title: What Really Happens to a Heat Pump at 0°F

scenes.purpose: Set the scene: the coldest night, the heat pump still running.

visual.description: Deep blue field; "The coldest night" settles in large type, frost-white, as the sentence begins.

scenes.narration: Picture the coldest night of a northern winter: frost on the windows, and the heat pump outside still humming.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers, and promise measurements.

visual.description: The question types on, centred; "very expensive space heater" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: Still heating, or a very expensive space heater?

scenes.narration: Is it still heating the house, or has it turned into a very expensive space heater? Meters, not marketing, can settle this.

scenes.purpose: Give the doubt in the headline's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "Falls Flat In The Cold" turns red as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "Taxpayers On The Hook For Tech That Falls Flat In The Cold"

scenes.narration: An NH Patch headline put the doubt bluntly: "Taxpayers On The Hook For Tech That Falls Flat In The Cold".

scenes.purpose: Give the opposite claim in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "-15 °F" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "many provide efficient heat at outdoor temperatures as low as -15 °F"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: The Mass Save heat pump page answers that "many provide efficient heat at outdoor temperatures as low as -15 °F".

scenes.purpose: Restate the question as the two options the evidence will choose between.

visual.description: The question types on; "give up" in red, "carry on" in green.
onScreenText: Give up in the cold, or carry on?

scenes.direction: Hold a beat before the investigation.
scenes.narration: So does a heat pump give up in the cold, or carry on as if nothing happened?

scenes.purpose: Introduce COP and the baseline of 1 for resistance heat.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the question first, then "Resistance heat: COP 1" with the 1 held large.

scenes.narration: Start with the bluntest question: does the heat keep coming at all? Engineers score heating efficiency as a COP, and plain electric resistance heat scores 1.

scenes.purpose: Show the metered mini-splits beat resistance heat even at -10 to 0 °F.

visual.description: Three tiles: resistance heat COP 1, metered mini-splits COP 1.5, and 50% more heat per unit of electricity; each lands as it is spoken.

chart.title: Heating efficiency at -10 to 0 °F

points.label: More heat per unit of electricity

chart.note: Average over dozens of metered units in the 2016 winter; the snowy 2015 winter ran less efficiently.

scenes.narration: In one evaluation, engineers metered the heat that dozens of ductless mini-splits delivered over back-to-back winters, and in the later one the units averaged a COP of 1.5 between -10 and 0 °F. That is 50 percent more heat per unit of electricity than resistance heat, which the evaluators called far superior; in the earlier winter, with deep snow and ice around the outdoor units, the units ran less efficiently.

scenes.purpose: Note the ordinary models also kept running below zero.

visual.description: One line; "below 0 °F" holds in ice blue.

scenes.narration: And not only the cold-climate models: the ordinary ones in that evaluation also ran below 0 °F, just less efficiently.

scenes.purpose: Show the prototype field COP against the Energy Star bar.

visual.description: Two tiles: median field COP 1.9 at 0 to 5 °F, then the Energy Star requirement 1.75 at 5 °F beside it.

chart.title: Prototype cold-climate heat pumps in the field
chart.note: Excludes periods with backup heat or defrost; the prototypes tested better in the lab.

citations.label: PNNL, 2025 cold-climate heat pump field test

scenes.narration: A newer field test followed prototype cold-climate heat pumps, and leaving out the periods when backup heat or defrost was running, their median COP between 0 and 5 °F was 1.9. Those prototypes tested better in the lab, but in the field most still beat 1.75, the COP the EPA's Energy Star label requires of a cold-climate heat pump at 5 °F.

scenes.purpose: Turn from efficiency to output.

visual.description: Split field: "Efficiency" on the left dims, "Output" on the right lights up.

scenes.narration: So the heat keeps coming. But efficiency is only half of it.

scenes.purpose: Name the second effect in a channel's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "heat output also drops" turns amber.
onScreenText: "along with getting less efficient, their actual heat output also drops."

scenes.narration: As the channel Technology Connections puts it, "along with getting less efficient, their actual heat output also drops."

scenes.purpose: Show how far one unit's output fell in extreme cold.

visual.description: One large tile: about 20% of rated output at -20 °F and colder, landing on "20 percent".

chart.title: One ductless unit, northern Minnesota

points.label: Output at -20 to -25 °F, share of its rating at 5 °F

chart.note: One unit; output held steady from 10 °F down to -15 °F.

scenes.narration: In northern Minnesota, researchers watched one small ductless unit hold a steady median output from 10 °F all the way down to -15 °F. Below that it kept running at reduced output, and at -20 °F and colder it delivered only about 20 percent of what it was rated for at 5 °F.

scenes.purpose: Give the researchers' verdict on backup in their own words.

visual.description: The report passage scrolls in; the line about not using these units without backup highlights.

excerpt.highlight: reduction in capacity shows these units should not be used without backup at extreme

scenes.narration: The researchers' verdict was that units like it should not be used without backup below -15 °F.

scenes.purpose: Show efficiency falling with temperature.

visual.description: Two tiles: COP around 1.3 at 10 °F in cold blue, COP 3.0 to 4.5 on mild days in warm orange.

chart.title: Heat-pump-only COP, Minnesota
chart.note: Cycles at the same temperature varied; outdoor temperature had the largest effect.

citations.label: CEE, 2017 Minnesota cold-climate heat pump study

scenes.direction: Tile on "1.3", then the mild-day tile on "mild days".
scenes.narration: Efficiency follows the same slope: in the same Minnesota research, outdoor temperature had the biggest effect on COP, and heat-pump-only cycles managed only around 1.3 at 10 °F, less than half what they reached on mild days.

scenes.purpose: Explain defrost and why it cools the vents.

visual.description: The PNNL defrost passage scrolls in; the line about rejecting heat from the conditioned space highlights.

excerpt.highlight: rejects heat from the conditioned space to the outdoor air melting off the frost

scenes.narration: Then there is the frost. In cold, humid air, frost builds up on the outdoor coil, and to melt it the heat pump runs in reverse, pulling heat out of the house, which can cool the air coming out of the vents.

scenes.purpose: Size the defrost cost: small in the median, large at one site.

visual.description: Two tiles: median defrost share of energy 5% to 8%, then the outlier site's 16% of time in defrost in amber.

chart.title: Defrost in the prototype field test
chart.note: The 16% is time, not energy, and one site against an average of 5%.

scenes.narration: In the prototype field test, defrost used a median of 5 to 8 percent of the energy at the temperatures where it cost most, a small share, though one site spent 16 percent of its time in defrost.

scenes.purpose: Name the real catch.

visual.description: One line punches in; "backup heat" in red.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the real catch: backup heat.

scenes.purpose: Give the warning about backup strips in the speaker's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "destroy your electric bill" turns red.
onScreenText: "They'll also absolutely destroy your electric bill."

scenes.narration: When a heat pump's electric backup strips kick in, Jordan Dearden warns, "They'll also absolutely destroy your electric bill."

scenes.purpose: Show how often backup ran below 0 °F, and how few sites had that data.

visual.description: Two tiles: 25% of the time with backup on below 0 °F, and the 22 sites in the study, the second tile smaller.

chart.title: Backup heat in the prototype field test
chart.note: Only 8 and 11 of the 22 sites had data in the two coldest ranges.

scenes.direction: First tile on "25 percent", second on "22 sites".
scenes.narration: In the prototype test, the units ran mostly on the heat pump alone, even at the lowest temperatures, and backup-only operation was minimal above 0 °F. But in the coldest range with enough data, below 0 °F, backup elements were on 25 percent of the time, and only some of the 22 sites had enough data that cold.

scenes.purpose: Show backup started early because of the thermostat.

visual.description: One line; "30 to 35 °F" in amber.

scenes.narration: Some backup use came from the thermostat: backup heat began at around 30 to 35 °F, and the researchers expect it would start much lower without homeowners changing setpoints, or with smarter thermostat controls.

scenes.purpose: Show backup that came from a controls fault, in the report's words.

visual.description: The PNNL passage on defrost strategies scrolls in; the manufacturer's controls-problem line highlights.

excerpt.highlight: The manufacturer team indicated that this was a controls problem and not intended operation.

scenes.narration: Some came from faults: two sites fired up higher stages of backup heat during defrost, at least one did it in normal heating too, and the manufacturer called that a controls problem.

scenes.purpose: Show the heat-pump-first system still beat resistance heat at its coldest reading.

visual.description: One line; "-7 °F" in ice blue.

scenes.narration: In the Minnesota study's all-electric system, the resistance booster joined in below 30 °F, yet because the heat pump ran first, the whole system still beat plain resistance heat even at the coldest reading, around -7 °F.

scenes.purpose: Note the unit that would not run below 0 °F.

visual.description: One line; "below 0 °F" in red.
onScreenText: One compressor would not run below 0 °F

scenes.narration: In another field study, one site's compressor would not run below 0 °F at all, even with its lockout disabled, most likely because of an on-board control setting that cannot be adjusted in the field.

scenes.purpose: Show sizing flipping the bill.

visual.description: Two tiles: $182 a year saved in green for heating-load sizing, $96 a year more in red for cooling-load sizing.

chart.title: Median bill change, Minnesota
chart.note: Modelled estimates for high-efficiency heat pumps.

citations.label: Wilson et al., 2024 heat pump bill model

scenes.narration: Sizing matters too: one study estimated that in Minnesota a high-efficiency heat pump sized for the full heating load cut median bills by $182 a year, while one sized for the cooling load raised them by $96, because it leaned harder on electric resistance backup.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the bill: savings against propane or electric heat.

visual.description: One tile: estimated savings of 30% to 56% against propane or electric heat.

chart.title: Minnesota homes, against propane or electric heat
chart.note: Estimated from performance maps and typical weather, not metered bills.

scenes.narration: So what does all this do to the bill? For the Minnesota homes, which had heated with propane or electricity, the researchers used performance maps and typical Minnesota weather to estimate cost savings of 30 to 56 percent.

scenes.purpose: Show where the mini-splits broke even with gas and propane.

visual.description: One tile: the break-even outdoor temperature against 80% efficient gas, above 70 °F, in red; it dims as s35 turns to propane.

chart.title: Outdoor temperature above which the mini-splits beat gas
chart.note: At the energy prices of those winters; against propane they were cheaper at every temperature.

scenes.direction: Tile lands on "70"; it dims on "Against propane".
scenes.narration: Gas is harder to beat: at the prices of those winters, the mini-splits from the first evaluation cost less to run than an 80 percent efficient gas system only above 70 °F, which the evaluators said made them no direct replacement for gas. Against propane, they were cheaper at every temperature.

scenes.purpose: Show the cold-climate units' break-even, measured and on paper.

visual.description: Three tiles: measured cold-climate units above 58 °F, then the rated model at 40 °F and 28 °F, the paper tiles outlined rather than filled.

chart.title: Break-even with gas, cold-climate units
chart.note: The 28 and 40 °F figures are from a rating curve, not measurement.

scenes.direction: Measured tile on "58", paper tiles on "on paper".
scenes.narration: Even the measured units listed as cold-climate broke even with gas only above 58 °F; on paper, the rating curve of a then-current cold-climate model brought it down to between 28 and 40 °F.

scenes.purpose: Show the lifetime-cost model splitting by city.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: Toronto in green, Edmonton in amber.
onScreenText: Toronto: heat pumps with gas backup
Edmonton: cheap gas and the cold

scenes.narration: A cost model for Toronto and Edmonton that counts equipment as well as energy points the same way: in Toronto, standard heat pumps with gas backup came out the lowest-cost option for nearly all households, but in Edmonton that held only for some house types, and gas with air conditioning won the rest. The model's reasons were cheap gas and the cold itself, which makes heat pumps less efficient and calls on the backup more.

scenes.purpose: Return to the question.

visual.description: The question types on, centred.
onScreenText: Do heat pumps still work when it gets really cold?

scenes.narration: So do heat pumps still work when it gets really cold?

scenes.purpose: Answer: they kept heating; backup is the catch.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the first in green, the second in amber.

citations.label: Cadmus 2016; CEE 2018; NREL 2023; PNNL 2025 field tests

scenes.narration: In these field tests most units did: they kept heating below zero, with less efficiency and less output, and still got more heat from each unit of electricity than resistance heat. The catch is backup heat, which ran more as it got colder, and more where a unit was sized for cooling or its controls misbehaved.

scenes.purpose: Answer the money question by what the heat pump replaces.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: "Save money?" then "Against gas: it turns on the unit, climate and prices".
onScreenText: Against gas: it turns on the unit, the climate and prices

scenes.narration: And do they still save money? Against propane or electric heat, the studies here say yes on running costs, though the Minnesota researchers put retrofit paybacks at over 10 years unless the old system needs replacing; against gas, it turns on the unit, the climate and local prices, and for the mini-splits measured in the first evaluation, gas won.

scenes.purpose: State the limit of the evidence.

visual.description: One line, smaller and grey.

scenes.direction: Hold a beat after the line.
scenes.narration: Each of these field tests followed a limited number of units, so they show what heat pumps can do in the cold, not what every installation will.

scenes.purpose: Give the viewer three things to ask and do.

visual.description: Three lines build one per sentence, as a checklist.

scenes.direction: Each line ticks on as its sentence begins; hold the list at the end.
scenes.narration: If your winters bite, ask the installer whether the unit is a cold-climate model, and whether it is sized for your heating load or only for your cooling. Ask what temperature the backup is set to start at, then keep the thermostat steady and watch how often the backup comes on. And if you heat with gas, work out the break-even temperature at your own prices before you decide what the furnace is for.
